summary: Gives example SIP messages designed to push a SIP implementation hard, with odd but valid or invalid forms to test parsers. Implementers can use them to find bugs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives SIP implementations difficult example messages to process. Some are valid despite looking unusual, while others are malformed and should be handled without crashing.

questions: how to test a sip parser
is a percent sign an escape in sip
how do sip torture tests work
subtitle: Example SIP messages that test how parsers handle unusual, valid and invalid input

tldr.problem: SIP implementations can mishandle unusual but valid messages or fail unsafely on malformed ones. These cases have caused interoperability problems and can exercise code paths used by crafted input.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC supplies example messages and describes expected parser, transaction and application behavior, alongside notation for messages that are hard to print exactly.
tldr.outcome: The messages are non-normative examples and a starting point for a test plan, not a comprehensive set of tests or a SIP specification.

today: RFC 4475 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC states that it is not normative and is not a complete test plan.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope of the Test Messages
sections.content:
The RFC presents examples based on SIP version 2.0, as specified in RFC 3261. The messages were developed and refined at interoperability events. Some exercise only parsing; others also exercise transaction or application behavior.

The document is explicitly Informational and not normative for SIP. It does not try to cover every malformed or unusual message. It is a seed for a test plan, focused on cases that have caused interoperability problems or could have harmful results if handled incorrectly.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are intended to expose places where a SIP implementation may misread a message. They are useful starting cases, but passing them does not prove that an implementation handles every problem.

sections.title: How the RFC Represents Exact Messages
sections.content:
RFC page layout cannot always show a SIP message unambiguously. The document defines markup for long unfolded lines, non-printable octets and repeated strings. For example, <allOneLine> means concatenate the lines inside it without line breaks, and <hex> represents octets as hexadecimal pairs.

This markup uses tag-like notation but is not an XML format. An encoded archive in the appendix contains bit-exact forms of the example messages for resolving remaining ambiguity.
sections.plainLanguage: Some example messages are too long or contain characters that cannot be printed normally. The RFC uses simple marks to show how to reconstruct them and includes exact copies in an appendix.

sections.title: Valid Messages That Look Unusual
sections.content:
The valid parser tests include unusual whitespace and capitalization, folded lines, short and long header names, unknown headers, unusual but legal characters, long values and empty or unfamiliar response phrases. A receiver must accept messages the RFC identifies as well-formed. Unknown header fields are treated as values: proxies forward them unchanged and endpoints ignore them.

Several cases test the percent sign. It is an escape only where the SIP grammar defines an escaped form; for example, a method containing % is not decoded into a different method. The examples also cover escaped nulls, extra trailing octets in a UDP datagram, multiple transport types and multipart bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: Some messages are valid even when their spacing, capitalization or characters look strange. A parser must follow the SIP rules for each field instead of applying one general cleanup rule to the whole message.

sections.title: Malformed Messages and Safe Reactions
sections.content:
The invalid parser tests include extra separators, incorrect or conflicting content lengths, values outside legal ranges, unterminated quoted strings, invalid spacing in request lines and URIs, invalid dates and mismatched methods. The examples describe suitable responses, such as a 400 Bad Request for several malformed requests, a 505 Version Not Supported for an unsupported version, or discarding a response with an overlarge response code.

Some cases allow a liberal parser to repair an error, but it must not propagate invalid syntax when forwarding a message. For stream transports, a framing error may require waiting for more data or closing the connection. Across all cases, implementations must not break when input is malformed.
sections.plainLanguage: Malformed messages should lead to a controlled error or be discarded, not a parser failure. If an implementation tries to repair input, it must do so carefully and avoid forwarding broken syntax.

sections.title: Transaction, Application and Compatibility Cases
sections.content:
Some examples go beyond syntax. They test missing transaction identifiers, missing required headers, unknown URI schemes and extensions, unsupported content types, repeated single-value fields, and multiple content lengths. For a legal request with Max-Forwards set to zero, a proxy should stop forwarding it and return 483, while an endpoint processes it normally.

The collection also includes an INVITE using RFC 2543 syntax. RFC 3261 implementations that aim to preserve backward compatibility should accept it. In the security section, the RFC warns that crafted input is a common attack method and says these examples are not comprehensive.
sections.plainLanguage: Other tests check whether SIP elements make the right decision after parsing, such as stopping a request at a proxy when its hop count is zero. The examples also include an older message form for implementations that support backward compatibility.
